scope: The corrected Chanukah 24 section only: three paragraphs and 89 phrase pairs, ending with Job 22:28. The displaced material belongs to the separate complete Chanukah 25 edition.

assessments.assessment: The complete paragraph distinguishes continuing personal benefit from the Exodus, physical place as a basis for a miracle blessing, annual holiness revealed in Torah, Purim during prophecy, and the Sages’ perception of enduring Chanukah holiness. Resisei 56:26 directly explains the enduring spiritual deliverance and the unwritten Oral Torah dimension. Resisei 57:1 provides strong but overlapping corroboration; the two Ishbitz–Radzin candidates instead examine Esther’s written status or preparation for festival holiness. All four candidate decisions are supported.

The complete discussion grants ordinary legal and protective enactments before addressing the harder claim about establishing sanctity in time. Takanat 12:14–15 grounds the heavenly effectiveness of a ruling in Torah entrusted below and explicitly gives a calendar example; its Aher context remains visible in the English. Sod Yesharim makes the grant of human authority depend on recognizing prior divine holiness and voluntary divine accommodation. The comparisons are analogies, not assertions that calendar sanctification and Chanukah are one legal institution. Beit Yaakov’s prayer context and Mei HaShiloach’s personal-perfection context are accurately declined at this anchor.

Only the genuine 15 final phrase pairs are included. Nasso 6:1–3 develops safeguards, individual Oral Torah innovation and inward intention, and the whole community’s contribution. Its princes’ offerings give a specific account of human initiative. Tiferet Yosef Pekudei 6 directly explains both work by human hands and divine completion credited to the worker. The Bereshit, Peri Tzadik Pekudei, and Miketz candidates are relevant but introduce different organizing arguments; their stated non-addition reasons are accurate. Neither approved comparison attributes holiness independent of God to human action.

changes.before: But the miracle of Chanukah, which was deliverance from forced abandonment of the faith alone, was established only for praise and thanksgiving, without any bodily pleasure, because it was not a deliverance of bodies. Its commandment is the lighting of the lamp, for this is the essential deliverance: “Light” is Torah. It was therefore not given to be written, because it has no embodiment in a bodily garment in this world. It is like all Oral Torah, of which “you are not permitted to recite these matters in writing.” This deliverance remained fixed and enduring for generations, like every holiness of the appointed times that remains in that time forever. This holiness is solely the deliverance of the soul and intellect, so that they will not be defiled by the wisdom of foreigners, which opposes the wisdom of Israel’s Sages in Oral Torah.

changes.before: After this comes the account of the princes’ dedication offerings. This alludes to the essential power of renewal in Oral Torah: what a person originates from the heart. Each prince himself conceived in his heart the bringing of these quantities of offerings. As Midrash Rabbah, chapter 12, explains on “They brought their offering,” they all brought their entire offering on their own initiative on the first day; afterwards, by the divine word, each offered on his own appointed day. Scripture details for each individual prince the number of offerings and their meal offerings, and the weight of the vessels, although all offered equally. This appears superfluous, for it could have written that on the second day a particular prince offered the same number as the first, and similarly for all of them. From this Midrash Rabbah demonstrates that each had different intentions in his offering, and therefore Scripture details each separately. From this we can understand the power of renewal in Oral Torah: even if two people perform an act of identical form, each nevertheless has a distinct meaning and level according to the preparation of the heart in the inner matter. The words concern, above all, the intention of the heart.
